fullAnalysis: Toad and Luigi make Nintendo feel likely fast, but several game franchises have mascot-style characters, so the exact universe can still stay open for a moment.
Piranha Plant is useful because it widens the board from named people to creatures and enemy types, which is common in franchise category puzzles.
Bowser is the turning clue because he is such a Mario-specific villain anchor that the franchise becomes much more exact than a generic Nintendo read.
After that, Princess Peach, Luigi, Toad, and Piranha Plant all confirm the same Mario universe cleanly.
The answer was Characters in Super Mario.
The board works because it mixes character roles on purpose so you solve for the world first, not for hero-villain alignment.
solutionNarrative: Toad and Luigi gave me Nintendo right away, but the board still wanted a tighter franchise answer than that. Piranha Plant helped by reminding me the puzzle was happy to use creatures and enemy types too, not only named protagonists.
Bowser made the answer specific. Once the main Mario villain was on the board, Princess Peach and the rest all resolved into the Super Mario cast instead of a generic video-game lineup.

lessons.title: Franchise boards care more about world than role
lessons.body: A puzzle can mix heroes, villains, side characters, and enemy species as long as they all belong to the same fictional universe.

lessons.title: One iconic villain can confirm the whole cast
lessons.body: Bowser carries a lot of weight because he is strongly associated with Mario and makes the franchise much harder to misread.

lessons.title: Do not reject species clues too quickly
lessons.body: Piranha Plant is not a single named person, but it still counts because Pinpoint often uses recurring enemy types as franchise markers.
